item.title: China, Russia vow to deepen high-quality cooperation and mutual trust at heads of government meeting
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 23:44:00
China Russia Photo: Xinhua China stands ready to work with Russia to further consolidate political mutual trust and strengthen strategic communication and coordination for the continuous development of bilateral ties and cooperation, Chinese Premier Li Qiang said on Wednesday as he met with Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin during the 31st regular meeting of the two countries' heads of government in St. Petersburg. Following the meeting on Wednesday, the two heads of government inked the Joint Communique, with a package of cooperation agreements on trade, aerospace, science, technology and education also reached. According to a release by the Xinhua News Agency, both sides agreed that strategic guidance from the heads of state is an important guarantee for the steady development of China-Russia relations. China and Russia should take the important consensus of the two heads of state as the fundamental guide, advance cooperation in key areas such as economy and trade, investment, energy and resources, connectivity, aerospace, finance and industry, foster new drivers of development in frontier areas such as artificial intelligence, biotechnology and the digital economy, jointly ensure the success of the China-Russia Years of Education, strengthen people-to-people and cultural exchanges in tourism, culture, youth and media, stimulate the vitality of local cooperation, maintain close communication and coordination on multilateral affairs, and strive for more practical outcomes, according to the release. Analysts said the China-Russia heads of government meeting centers on delivering on the consensus reached by two heads of state and will lend key support to the high-quality upgrading of China-Russia cooperation. Meanwhile, amid a turbulent and complex international landscape, China and Russia's coordination helps steer the international order toward an equal and orderly multipolar world, reject bloc confrontation, hegemonism and unilateral sanctions, and galvanize development momentum for the Global South. Entering a new stage This year marks the 30th anniversary of the establishment of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. The annual meeting between Chinese and Russian heads of government was launched in 1996. During the meeting, Premier Li said that under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China-Russia relations are entering a new stage marked by greater achievements and faster development, the Xinhua News Agency reported. China and Russia set a model for high-level mutual trust and high-quality cooperation between major countries and neighboring countries in the new era, Li noted. Mishustin said the Russia-China comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for a new era is currently at its highest level in history and has set an example for relations between countries. Russia is willing to work with China on the basis of mutual benefit, win-win cooperation, mutual respect and good-neighborliness and friendship, to further strengthen practical cooperation in various fields and safeguard the common interests of the two countries, he added. According to Wang Xiaoquan, an expert with the Institute of Russian, Eastern European and Central Asian Studies of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, the core functions of the regular heads-of-government meeting mechanism are to focus on practical cooperation, translate consensus reached by the two heads of state into actionable government policies, projects and institutional arrangements, review their implementation, and coordinate policies among government ministries and local authorities on both sides. Wan Qingsong, an expert at the Center for Russian Studies at East China Normal University, said the mechanism provides crucial underpinning for the high-quality development of China-Russia relations. With China set to host the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen this November, this heads-of-government meeting also lays groundwork and creates more favorable conditions for a possible summit between the two heads of state. In 2026, China and Russia have maintained frequent high-level interactions, with two heads of state holding fruitful meetings in May and August. Top legislator Zhao Leji and top diplomat Wang Yi also met with their Russian counterparts. During Russian President Vladimir Putin's state visit to China in May, the two heads of state signed and issued a joint statement on further enhancing comprehensive strategic coordination and deepening good-neighborliness and friendly cooperation between the two countries. The two leaders witnessed the signing of 20 cooperation documents in areas including the economy and trade, education, and science and technology. The two sides also reached 20 cooperation agreements in other fields. Wang Xiaoquan said China and Russia uphold the principles of non-alliance, non-confrontation and not targeting any third party. They enjoy strong political mutual trust and strategic rapport, backed by a full-fledged cooperation framework and strong endogenous momentum for sustainable development. According to the expert's observation, China-Russia practical cooperation is shifting from expansion in scale to quality upgrading. Energy, cross-border logistics and agricultural and forestry trade remain the ballast, while high-tech sectors, the digital economy, equipment manufacturing investment, local currency settlement, green and low-carbon development, as well as subnational and border cooperation have emerged as new growth drivers. From 2023 to 2025, bilateral China-Russia trade exceeded $200 billion for three straight years, with China retaining its status as Russia's top trading partner for 16 consecutive years. Data from the General Administration of Customs of China shows that bilateral trade hit $134.175 billion in the first half of this year, a year-on-year increase of 25.6 percent. Side by side The latest China-Russia heads of government engagement came after their attendance of the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Dushanbe, Tajikistan, on Tuesday. In his talks with Mishustin, Premier Li said that China and Russia in recent years have stood side by side and moved forward together amid a complex and turbulent international landscape, Xinhua reported. Upon his arrival in St. Petersburg on Tuesday, Li said China and Russia's effort will not only bring greater benefits to the two peoples and inject valuable stability and certainty into world peace and development, according to Xinhua's release. The international landscape is volatile with intensifying conflicts and fragmented industrial and supply chains, said Wan, adding that the global governance system is undergoing profound shifts. Against such a backdrop, Russia and China enjoy broad room for coordination. The two sides can boost synergy among multilateral frameworks, pool strengths, advance regional economic and trade connectivity, and keep global industrial and supply chains stable, Wan noted. China will host the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen this November and assume the rotating chairmanship of BRICS in 2027. During a meeting with Chinese top diplomat Wang Yi in Baku in October, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said that Russia fully supports China in successfully hosting the APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting. In addition, Russia is ready to further strengthen coordination with China under multilateral frameworks including the United Nations, the G20, APEC and the BRICS mechanism to jointly uphold international fairness and justice, he said. "By advancing cooperation, China and Russia can not only jointly fend off external risks, but also steer the international order toward an equal and orderly multipolar world, galvanize development momentum for the Global South, and reject bloc confrontation, hegemonism and unilateral sanctions," said Wang Xiaoquan. "Their multilateral coordination serves both regional stability and global governance. It shuns bloc rivalry and provides a practical, viable pathway for cooperation in a turbulent world," the expert noted.

item.title: Long March spirit sails on in China's modern navy
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 23:32:00
A photo released by the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Navy on August 6, 2026, shows the moment when a J-15 fighter jet took off from the aircraft carrier Liaoning amid sunset hues. Photo: WeChat account of the PLA Navy From nuclear-powered submarines beneath the waves to destroyers on the open sea, names that originated in China's Long March now travel far beyond the routes once taken by the Red Army in the 1930s. The name Changzheng, or Long March, has become the hallmark of China's nuclear submarines, while warships named Zunyi, Chishui and Aba, important places along routes of the Long March, carry reminders of the epic journey into today's naval missions. Ahead of Thursday's 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March, China's military is reflecting on how that experience helped shape its direction and development. Experts said the legacy lives on in the equipment China builds: the pursuit of independent innovation and the determination to overcome formidable obstacles give these historic names a meaning that extends beyond remembrance. That connection stretches from Long March-1, China's first nuclear-powered submarine, commissioned in 1974, to the third generation of Long March nuclear submarines and a recently reported strategic missile test by a nuclear-powered submarine, according to a report by the Xinhua News Agency. Alongside them, successive generations of surface warships have carried the names of places associated with the Long March, linking the navy's expanding capabilities with its revolutionary heritage. History carried to sea The Long March was an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that broke through the encirclement of Kuomintang forces. Red Army soldiers braved raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and treacherous grasslands, with some marching as far as 12,500 kilometers. The maneuver helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution. Ruijin, Zunyi, Chishui, Aba and Liupanshan are some of the places associated with that arduous undertaking, which culminated with the joining of the Red Army's main forces in October 1936. Nine decades later, its influence can be traced in a very different setting: China's naval fleet. China's Long March nuclear submarines have developed to a third generation, and a Long March nuclear submarine has had a successful test launch of a submarine-launched strategic missile, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Saturday. This evolution follows a path that began with the country's first nuclear submarine entering service in 1974. According to CCTV News, the name Long March was adopted following a worker's suggestion. It reflected the difficulties overcome in developing the submarine and symbolized its endurance and ability to undertake missions in distant waters. The name subsequently became a defining feature of China's nuclear submarine force. The development of China's strategic nuclear submarines has focused on quieter operations, greater stealth and survivability, improved diving performance and greater diving depths, Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Wednesday. He also pointed to the pursuit of greater missile capacity and longer missile ranges. Naming the submarines after the Long March honors that history and carries forward a commitment to overcoming hardship, making sacrifices and following a path of self-reliance, Zhang said. It reflects the circumstances in which Chinese military equipment was developed, with external technological restrictions compounded by a weak domestic industrial base at the time. Overcoming those barriers required a determination comparable to that of the Long March, Zhang said. The name therefore connects the difficulties of the revolutionary journey with the challenges faced by generations of equipment developers. That connection also runs through the names of surface warships. Li Junjie, an associate professor at the School of History and Culture of the Minzu University of China, told the Global Times on Wednesday that many names in the military's equipment buildup draw on places associated with the Long March. Zunyi in Guizhou Province is associated with the conference that marked a pivotal turning point in the history of the Communist Party of China, and it has lent its name to two generations of destroyers, Li said. The succession allows the historical memory embodied in the name to continue as the ships themselves evolve. The current Zunyi is an independently developed and built Type 055 guided-missile destroyer of a 10,000-ton class. Since entering service, it has undertaken combat-readiness patrols, maritime rights-protection operations and joint exercises involving multiple services and branches, according to Chinese media reports. It spends more than 200 days at sea annually on average and has sailed nearly 180,000 nautical miles. Its predecessor, a Type 051 guided-missile destroyer also named Zunyi, was decommissioned in 2019 after more than 30 years of service, according to China's Defense Ministry. Zhang said that People's Liberation Army Navy's Type 055 destroyers have strong far seas capabilities, citing their strong air and missile defense capabilities and their ability to engage surface ships, submarines and land targets. In the future, he said, the Long March spirit will continue to encourage equipment development toward greater use of intelligent technologies and unmanned systems, strengthening the PLA Navy's ability to perform diverse missions and conduct integrated combat operations. Students from Linze county No.4 Middle School listen to stories of the heroic Long March of the Red Army at a memorial hall in Zhangye, Northwest China's Gansu Province on October 21, 2026. Photo: VCG A legacy renewed after 90 years The anniversary has also prompted reflection on the lessons that reach beyond the equipment itself. An article published on the Ministry of National Defense website on Wednesday examined what the Long March can teach today's military, emphasizing Party leadership, the motivating power of political mobilization and lessons for national defense mobilization. The article recalled the severe conditions confronting the Red Army: encirclement and interception while outnumbered greatly by enemy forces, harsh natural environments, scattered and limited local support, and acute shortages of supplies and equipment. Under the CPC's leadership, the Red Army adopted different mobilization strategies to secure personnel, material and financial resources, while winning support from the people. That experience demonstrated that Party leadership is essential to keeping wartime mobilization on the right course, while political mobilization provides a powerful source of motivation for military victory, the article said. It called for using the implementation of the newly revised National Defense Mobilization Law to further develop a framework in which the Party exercises overall leadership, the military identifies the requirements and the government implements them. Under unified Party leadership, military and civilian authorities should fulfill their respective responsibilities while coordinating closely, it said. A Xinhua editorial on Tuesday described the Long March spirit as a precious legacy forged through the sacrifices of CPC members and Red Army soldiers. It placed the fundamental interests of the Chinese people and nation above all else, and stressed the willingness to confront hardship and make sacrifices to save the country and its people. The editorial also highlighted independence, seeking truth from facts and acting according to actual conditions, as well as paying attention to the overall situation, strict discipline and unity, and close reliance on the people, sharing their hardships and persevering together. For Li, firm ideals and convictions form the main part of what the Long March left to China's military. "Passed down through generations, this revolutionary heritage helps unite thought and action, purpose and strength, shaping a people's military defined by discipline, conviction and a sense of responsibility," he said. From military organization to equipment development, each era adds to the meaning of the Long March spirit by applying it to new circumstances, Li said. The names remain familiar, but the task of carrying their legacy forward is renewed with each generation. "Every era has its own understanding of the Long March," Li said. "What matters is drawing strength from it and continuing to move forward."

item.title: Chinese scientists confirm Xujiayao hominins as Denisovans, revealing shared physical traits
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 23:09:00
Photo: Courtesy of Fu Qiaomei Chinese scientists have identified the Xujiayao hominins, whose fossils were unearthed in North China’s Hebei Province, as Denisovans, a distinct branch of ancient humans, through palaeoproteomic analyses and morphological comparisons, revealing shared physical traits of Denisovans, a breakthrough in resolving a long-standing debate over the classification of archaic humans in East Asia during the late Middle Pleistocene, the Global Times learned from the research team on Wednesday. The study was published in the international journal Nature on Wednesday. First identified in 2010 through DNA analysis of a finger bone discovered in Denisova Cave in Siberia, Denisovans are now known to have inhabited a wide area spanning northeastern East Asia, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, southwestern and southeastern China, and parts of Southeast Asia from around 300,000 to 45,000 years ago, possibly later. However, despite growing fossil and molecular evidence, scientists have struggled to establish clear morphological criteria for identifying Denisovans. Identifying shared Denisovan traits requires an ideal archaeological site with molecularly confirmed Denisovan remains, abundant human fossils, well-defined stratigraphic context and reliable dating. The Xujiayao hominins, dating to 199,000 to 138,000 years ago, have recently been classified as Homo longi, a group that includes Siberian Denisovans. Excavations at the Xujiayao site from 1976 to 1979 unearthed 20 human fossils, including cranial remains, mandibles and teeth, representing at least 16 individuals at different stages of life, making it one of the hominin sites in East Asia with the clearest stratigraphic records and richest fossil assemblages from the late Middle Pleistocene. If the Xujiayao hominins are confirmed to be Denisovans, the discovery would clarify their taxonomic status, help establish the shared morphological traits among Denisovans, and address gaps in research on Denisovans compared with Neanderthals and modern humans. To clarify this question, a joint research team led by Fu Qiaomei and Xing Song, both are researchers at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with researchers from Nanjing Normal University, Peking University and other institutions, conducted palaeoproteomic and morphological analyses of the Xujiayao hominin fossils. The findings have provided clear evidence that the Xujiayao hominins belong to the Denisovan lineage. Building on these findings, the team has identified key Denisovan traits in the skull, jaw and teeth, including primitive features resembling those of Homo erectus and more derived characteristics shared with later members of the genus Homo. These include a low, broad cranial vault, thick skull bones, short mastoid processes, and simplified premolar chewing surfaces. Although the Xujiayao fossils lack facial remains, evidence from comparable fossils unearthed at other sites suggests that Denisovans had low, receding foreheads, prominent brow ridges, flat faces and less pronounced jaw protrusion. Using molecularly confirmed Xujiayao fossils as a reference, the study has identified shared Denisovan traits in the skull, jaw and teeth, establishing the first morphology-based identification framework for the group in the 16 years since discovery. This finding advances Denisovans from a mysterious group identified primarily through molecular evidence to an ancient human group that can be recognized, compared and classified based on morphological characteristics, fundamentally deepening people’s understanding of the pattern of human evolution in East Asia during the Middle Pleistocene.

item.title: The Philippines should not misread the message of US warship's intrusion near Xianbin Jiao: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:59:00
The Philippines Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The US warship's early-morning "quick in, quick out" and the limited tonnage of a littoral combat ship themselves demonstrate that the priority of this performance was "risk control" rather than "deterrence effect." Any calculation that drawing in outside forces can help seize gains in the South China Sea is a serious misjudgment of the situation; any act that infringes on China's sovereignty and rights will be met with resolute countermeasures. In the early hours of Tuesday, the US littoral combat ship USS Charleston illegally intruded into the waters adjacent to Xianbin Jiao of China's Nansha Qundao without approval from the Chinese government. The People's Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command Navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the US vessel in accordance with laws and regulations. A spokesperson for the PLA Southern Theater Command Navy stated clearly that China holds indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters. The US' action infringes upon China's sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability. The US side should immediately cease such activities. Xianbin Jiao lies to the east of Ren'ai Jiao. In recent years the Philippines has continuously taken infringement actions in the direction of Xianbin Jiao, hyped up the so-called "environmental issue" at Xianbin Jiao and dispatched coast guard vessels to illegally linger in its lagoon. These various moves have failed under China's countermeasures. At this moment, the US sent a littoral combat ship to intrude in the early morning. The action was carefully designed. The US warship's early-morning "quick in, quick out" and the limited tonnage of a littoral combat ship themselves demonstrate that the priority of this performance was "risk control" rather than "deterrence effect." So-called "freedom of navigation" is a false proposition in the South China Sea. The US' "freedom of navigation operations" are by no means intended to safeguard genuine freedom of navigation. Fifty percent of the world's merchant ships and one-third of maritime trade pass through the South China Sea. No matter how complex the disputes, normal international commercial navigation in the South China Sea has never been obstructed. What has truly turned "freedom of navigation" into an issue is not the passage needs of merchant ships, but the close-in disruptive actions of warships carrying specific political intentions. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) has still not clearly stipulated whether foreign warships enjoy the right of "innocent passage." Yet many countries require that foreign warships obtain approval or provide prior notification before entering their territorial seas. China also made relevant provisions in its 1992 Law on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone. Yet the US has not joined UNCLOS to this day, while believing that it has the "right to interpret" the Convention's concepts - this is itself a paradox. Observing the reactions of the US and the Philippines before and after the incident, one intruded and the other cheered. The US side trotted out its usual "freedom of navigation" rhetoric, while the Philippine side claimed that "the US warship did not intrude into Chinese territory." These "concerted performances" carried out in the name of fulfilling security commitments and upholding rules and order resemble a carefully choreographed parade, reflecting that the "display of allied strength" by the Philippines and the US in the South China Sea is nothing more than a publicity project staged around so-called "security issues." To some extent, such activities have become a "mobile billboard" for the US to showcase the credibility of its alliances. The audience this performance is aimed at may be other US allies and partners in the Asia-Pacific, proclaiming US military dominance in the region, but China remains an unavoidable "presence" in this performance. Anti-China forces within the Philippine military and police systems are now wantonly undermining China-Philippines relations. Behind this there is the backing and cheerleading of external forces, as well as the acquiescence and indulgence of the Philippine government. These people regard US "freedom of navigation" operations in the South China Sea as chips for gaming with China and for bargaining. But Manila needs to understand that external major powers will not bear the cost of direct conflict with China for the Philippines' adventurous actions, nor will they underwrite Manila when the situation gets out of control. They can withdraw at any time, and the Philippines will have to clean up the mess itself. Disputes in the South China Sea should be resolved through consultation among countries in the region; No external force has the right to intervene. This is a principle China has consistently upheld, and it is the only correct path for maintaining long-term peace and stability in the South China Sea. The Philippine side is advised not to misread the situation and mistake a performance for a "backer." The fact that this incident occurred in the early morning proves that any unauthorized infringement and intrusion is under China's monitoring and control. The Southern Theater Command Navy possesses all-weather situational awareness and rapid-response capabilities in the South China Sea, and is able to promptly detect, grasp, and handle relevant developments. China has indisputable sovereignty over the Nansha Qundao and their adjacent waters, and the Theater Command forces remain on high alert at all times. Manila needs to see clearly that the early-morning "quick in, quick out" performance by the US warship is not proof that "someone has its back," but rather a preview that "risks must be borne by oneself." Any calculation that drawing in outside forces can help seize gains in the South China Sea is a serious misjudgment of the situation; any act that infringes on China's sovereignty and rights will be met with resolute countermeasures.

item.title: China to improve detection of magnitude 1.0-2.5 earthquakes under 15th Five-Year Plan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:40:00
An illustration of a user interface of earthquake warning system. Photo: VCG China will further improve its earthquake monitoring network during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), with the goal of enabling the country to detect earthquakes of magnitude 1.0 to 2.5 across different regions, China Central Television (CCTV) News reported on Wednesday, citing information released at a State Council Information Office press conference. According to the report, China will establish dense geophysical observation networks in key areas to monitor ground deformation, fluids and electromagnetic activity. Deep-well observation stations will also be built in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and other regions to obtain scientific data with higher precision and greater spatial and temporal resolution, enhancing the ability to detect earthquake signals. China will also build seismic observation stations in coastal waters and densify the network of seismic monitoring stations in southwestern and northwestern regions, expanding the coverage of seismic monitoring in offshore areas and western China. Various specialized seismic networks will be integrated into the national monitoring system, CCTV News reported. Earthquake monitoring capability is a key indicator in earthquake prevention and disaster reduction. It measures the smallest-magnitude earthquake that a region's seismic network can accurately record. The lower the magnitude threshold, the greater the monitoring capability, the CCTV report explained. Earthquakes below magnitude 3 are generally difficult for people to feel unless they occur at shallow depths. The latest plan builds on China's existing earthquake monitoring and early warning infrastructure. China completed its National Earthquake Early Warning Project in July 2024, establishing a network of 15,899 observation stations across the country, according to a report from the Xinhua News Agency. At the time, authorities said the network could detect earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or above in most parts of the country, magnitude 2.0 or above in eastern regions and magnitude 1.0 or above in densely populated areas including the Beijing metropolitan area and the Yangtze River Delta. For comparison, Natural Resources Canada says its seismic network can detect all earthquakes with magnitude exceeding 3 in eastern Canada, with the detection threshold reaching magnitude 2.5 or greater in densely populated areas. In the US, the US Geological Survey (USGS) lists a detection threshold of magnitude 1.0 or greater for a seismic monitoring network near Parkfield, California. Global Times

item.title: Takaichi's first year in office marked by unfulfilled pledges, lopsided diplomacy amid regional tensions: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:57:00
People protest during a rally in Tokyo, Japan, Oct. 20, 2026. Japanese citizens staged a protest rally in front of the Ministry of Defense in Tokyo on Tuesday evening, opposing the large-scale Japan-U.S. joint military exercises and the military buildup. (Xinhua/Li Ziyue) Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi marked one year in office on Wednesday amid Japanese media scrutiny of her performance, particularly strained ties with China. Her administration has fallen short on promises of economic revival and social stability, while its lopsided diplomacy and risky push to cast aside Japan's pacifist constitutional constraints are fueling regional tensions and making Japan a source of instability in the region, a Chinese expert said. Speaking to reporters at the Prime Minister's Office on Wednesday afternoon, Takaichi defended her record and claimed "I have kept going throughout this past year with the conviction that my mission is to steadily deliver on each of my promises," according to the Asahi Shimbun. She said tackling rising prices would remain her top priority, alongside strengthening intelligence capabilities and pursuing changes to security policy. Japanese media reviews, however, highlighted mounting economic pressures, divisions within her administration and diplomatic setbacks, particularly in relations with China. Jiji Press reported on Wednesday that the Japanese prime minister hopes to build a record of achievements to secure reelection as Liberal Democratic Party president next autumn. "At home, however, public frustration over rising prices is growing, while her diplomacy appears increasingly deadlocked, particularly in relations with China. Cabinet approval ratings, a key source of her political strength, are also showing signs of weakening, leaving her once-dominant position increasingly uncertain," according to the report. In an editorial published on Tuesday, the Mainichi Shimbun also noted that Takaichi's arbitrary approach had deepened divisions and that her intransigence was undermining governance. Her return to an "economy first" stance sought to replenish political capital spent forcing through conservative policies, but results had fallen short of her rhetoric. The yen has continued to weaken since her administration took office, with no sign of relief from rising prices. Diplomatically, she had largely followed US President Donald Trump's lead amid the global turmoil he had triggered and failed to find an opening to repair ties with China following her remarks on a potential "Taiwan contingency," said the editorial. Takaichi's administration has made little progress in delivering on its economic pledges. Rising government bond yields and persistent inflation have exposed the limits of its policies, while deteriorating ties with China have added to the pressure, Lü Chao, a research fellow at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times. Rather than offering effective solutions to these pressures, the Takaichi government has continued to increase defense spending, expand Japan's military capabilities, ease restrictions on arms exports and pursue revisions to the country's postwar pacifist Constitution, he said. Attempting to stimulate growth through military expansion amounts to "drinking poison to quench thirst," diverting resources from public wellbeing, leaving pledges to improve livelihoods unfulfilled and fueling public opposition in Japan. Japanese citizens staged a protest rally in front of the National Diet in Tokyo on Monday evening, opposing the military buildup and constitutional revision drive of Takaichi's government and calling for the preservation of peace. Protesters chanted slogans including "Stop blindly following the US," "Stop deploying long-range missiles," and "Takaichi must step down immediately," according to the Xinhua News Agency. On foreign policy, Takaichi is postwar Japan's most blatant right-wing prime minister, Lü said. Shortly after taking office, her remarks on the so-called "Taiwan contingency" had challenged China's red lines. Her refusal to change course throughout her first year has driven China-Japan relations to a low point, with little prospect of improvement. A Jiji Press report on Wednesday also highlighted Japan's diplomatic impasse, including its relations with Russia, North Korea and China. It noted that at a House of Councillors Budget Committee meeting on October 16, Kiyomi Tsujimoto of the Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan mocked Takaichi's pledge to pursue "Japanese diplomacy that flourishes at the center of the world," asking whether Japan might instead "be relegated to a corner of the world." Lü noted that over the past year, the Takaichi government's aggressive military buildup and push for arms exports have echoed Japan's militarist past and are bound to raise alarm among both its Asian neighbors and the wider international community. Failed economic and livelihood policies, lopsided diplomacy and reckless security moves are also making Japan a source of instability in the Asia-Pacific, Lü said.

item.title: Is Elon Musk building a 'flying car' because he has been 'pushed out' of traditional auto race by China?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:47:00
Chinese NEVs Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Editor's Note: Currently, China's economy is steadily advancing along the path of high-quality development, even as domestic and international circumstances become increasingly complex. Some Western media, due to misunderstanding or bias, have repeatedly questioned or even distorted China's economic development. Accordingly, the Global Times launches the "Q&A on China's Economy" column to publish opinion pieces to present facts and clarify perceptions. Tesla recently unveiled its next-generation Roadster, which can briefly take flight and perform an aerial flip, drawing global attention. The Wall Street Journal published an article arguing that "Elon Musk's latest vision for the company's sports car has more to do with China than cold-gas rocket thrusters." It suggested that Musk "is leaving the mainstream car market to the Chinese" because "many Western automakers are unable to compete without government intervention." The article also claimed that some Western automakers are feeling the same pressure as Musk to either "move up" or "be pushed out." But does the rise of China's auto industry really mean that automakers from other countries are being forced off the track? The competitive pressure generated by China's auto industry is indeed a reality that automakers around the world cannot ignore. Musk himself has publicly described Chinese automakers as the "most competitive in the world." According to the International Energy Agency, global electric vehicle sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with Chinese automakers accounting for around 60 percent of sales and roughly three-quarters of global EV production. At this year's Paris Motor Show, the presence of more than 20 Chinese auto brands attracted considerable attention in Europe. Chinese companies have evolved from important participants in the global auto industry into formidable competitors in an expanding range of markets and technological fields. However, interpreting Tesla's Roadster unveiling as a simple retreat from the mainstream market is misleading. From the outset, the Roadster was designed for a niche market, serving as a showcase for Tesla's technological capabilities and brand image. It is not just Tesla. In recent years, nearly all leading global automakers have placed greater emphasis on autonomous driving, connected vehicles and AI applications, reflecting a broader industry consensus on the future of mobility and automotive technology. In fact, most established automakers have not abandoned the mass market. On the contrary, they are stepping up efforts to compete for this core segment of the automotive market. Volkswagen and Renault are still developing more affordable electric vehicles and Toyota and Honda are maintaining dual-track strategies involving both hybrids and pure electric vehicles. The transformation underway in the global auto industry is therefore far more complex than a scenario in which Chinese companies take over the mass market while Western automakers retreat to the premium segment. To understand this transformation, it is essential to examine the sources of China's automotive competitiveness. Technological innovation in the auto industry has often followed a pattern in which new technologies are introduced in premium models before gradually spreading to ordinary vehicles. The more advanced the technology, the higher the price tends to be. As the technology matures and becomes more widely available, features once reserved for high-end cars eventually find their way into more affordable models. The intense competition in China's auto market is accelerating this process. In 2025, around 70 percent of the battery electric vehicles sold in China were priced below the average price of conventional gasoline cars. Smart cockpits, advanced driver-assistance systems, efficient electric drivetrains and ultra-fast charging are increasingly available in vehicles that ordinary consumers can afford. Whether Musk's "flying sports car" will ever prove practical remains to be seen. China's auto industry, however, has already demonstrated that new technologies need not be reserved for a privileged few; they can also benefit the wider public. The fundamental strength of China's auto industry lies in its ability to closely integrate technological innovation, large-scale manufacturing and market demand, enabling advanced technologies to be translated into products more quickly and made accessible to more consumers. This is underpinned by the country's long-developed industrial ecosystem. Close coordination across the power battery, electric motor, electronic controls and intelligent manufacturing sectors allows automakers to iterate technologies and develop new products more rapidly. China's vast domestic market provides a wealth of real-world application scenarios, while consumers' growing demand for intelligent and electrified vehicles continues to push companies to improve their products. Chinese automakers also face intense competition, and a number of new-energy vehicle companies have already been eliminated in recent years. Yet it is this competitive environment that has helped drive greater industrial efficiency and innovation, propelling the sector to the forefront of the global industry. Seen in this light, portraying the growth of China's auto industry as "swallowing up markets" deliberately amplifies the perceived threat of competition while overlooking the new opportunities and changes that healthy competition can create. Tesla's entry into China injected fresh competition into the domestic market, producing a "catfish effect" that spurred local manufacturers to improve. The establishment of Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory also put pressure on Chinese automakers, but Chinese suppliers gained technical expertise and experience through production partnerships, improving both efficiency and quality. This has been a process of mutual development. Today, cooperation between Chinese and international automakers, such as Xpeng and Volkswagen, as well as Geely and Ford, further demonstrates how the global auto industry is building new networks of innovation. More than a century of automotive history has been a story of competition driving innovation and technology becoming increasingly accessible. The US once revolutionized the industry through mass production; Japanese automakers raised efficiency through lean manufacturing; and European carmakers built deep strengths in technology and branding. Today, the rise of China's auto industry is adding a new chapter to that history. Rather than treating market competition as a zero-sum game in which one side's gains must come at the other's expense, automakers should focus on strengthening their competitiveness through innovation and cooperation. China's automotive rise has not deprived the global auto industry of a future. On the contrary, it has opened up more possibilities for the industry's future.

item.title: China's cumulative carbon emission trading volume exceeds 1 billion tonnes; country offers insights for global action addressing climate change
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:13:00
An aerial drone photo taken on June 3, 2026 shows a farming-photovoltaic power complementary project in Huimin County, Binzhou City, East China's Shandong Province. Photo: VCG China has established the world's largest carbon emissions trading market, with cumulative trading volume in its national carbon emissions trading market surpassing one billion tonnes, an official from the Ministry of Ecology and Environment said on Wednesday, highlighting it as one of China's key achievements in tackling climate change. The figures were released at a press conference on Wednesday ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which will be held in Antalya, Turkey, from November 9 to 20. A Chinese expert said China's sustained efforts in climate action can offer valuable experience for other countries. In just over five years, China has established the world's largest carbon emissions trading market, covering about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, or more than 65 percent of the country's total emissions , said Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, during the press conference held by the State Council Information Office, per Xinhua. In terms of emissions reduction and efficiency gains, China helped reduce carbon dioxide emissions from the thermal power sector by approximately 530 million tonnes during the 14th Five-Year Plan period (2021-25). Internationally, China's carbon market has received widespread recognition for its achievements and has become an important platform for showcasing the country's efforts to address climate change, the CCTV report said. During the same conference, Li also said that China will send a delegation to attend COP31 and will actively advance international climate negotiations. COP31 will conduct negotiations and consultations on nearly 100 agenda items related to the implementation of the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, covering mitigation, adaptation, finance and just transition, per CCTV News. "As a responsible major developing country, China has consistently participated in and advanced international climate negotiations in a proactive and constructive manner," Li said, adding that China will contribute Chinese wisdom, solutions and strength to the success of COP31. Ma Jun, director of the Institute of Public and Environmental Affairs, told the Global Times that the gap between emission reduction pledges and real action remains wide, with current global efforts falling short of global climate targets and climate overshoot increasingly unavoidable. Geopolitical divisions fragment global governance, hinder climate cooperation and complicate efforts to balance energy, food and climate security, he noted. Some developing countries also struggle to balance climate mitigation and adaptation with economic growth and poverty alleviation, constrained by severe shortages of finance, technology and capacity, Ma added. The expert noted that China's sustained climate action offers a valuable lesson by integrating emissions reduction with pollution control and green transformation. Linking clean energy, energy-efficiency upgrades and electric vehicles with environmental improvement, resource recycling, industrial upgrading and job creation can address climate change while creating new sources of green growth. Through South-South cooperation, China can help other developing countries strengthen their capacity for independent climate action and reduce transition costs by sharing appropriate technologies, project experience and training. These lessons should, of course, be adapted to each country's resource endowments and stage of development, Ma noted. Li said during the press conference on Wednesday that China has built the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth, according to a report by the Xinhua News Agency. By the first half of 2026, the country's total installed renewable energy capacity reached 2.46 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of total national power generation capacity. At the end of July, installed solar power capacity surpassed coal power for the first time in history, making it China's largest single power source. Moreover, China's combined installed capacity of operational and approved nuclear power units has risen to first place in the world. New energy vehicle production and sales have ranked first globally for 11 consecutive years. On Wednesday, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment also released an annual report on China's policies and actions for addressing climate change 2026, outlining China's basic position and proposals for the COP31. "China will continue to play a proactive and constructive role, support Turkey in its capacity as the COP31 Presidency and Australia as the President of Negotiations, and work with other Parties in the spirit of a community with a shared future for humanity to ensure that COP31 focuses on implementation and cooperation," it reads.

item.title: GT Voice: Chip export boom reveals deepening China-South Korea complementarity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 20:47:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT South Korea's exports are becoming a showcase of the global technology industry. During the first 20 days of October, South Korea's semiconductor exports surged 222.5 percent year-on-year to reach $27.5 billion, setting a new record. The chip exports accounted for 44.7 percent of the country's total, up 16.2 percentage points from a year earlier, the Yonhap News Agency reported on Wednesday. By destination, chip exports to China soared 154.4 percent to $16.6 billion, and exports to the US stood at $10.7 billion. Viewed over the longer term, this round of South Korea's export growth extends an AI-driven expansion of global computing demand that has been building for years. In 2024, South Korean chip exports rose to $141.9 billion, up 43.9 percent year-on-year. In 2025, the figure climbed to $173.4 billion, up 22.2 percent. South Korea's semiconductor exports have kept surging this year. In the first quarter, they reached $78.5 billion, up 139 percent year-on-year, and in the first half year, they hit $192.4 billion, exceeding the whole of 2025. The Bank of Korea in August raised the country's economic growth forecast this year to 3.3 percent - an increase of 0.7 percentage points and the highest level since 2021. The rationale behind this upward revision was that the extraordinary prosperity of South Korea's semiconductor sector was spreading from exports into domestic consumption, investment and other areas of local demand, steering the country's economy onto a more solid trajectory of growth. The massive jump in South Korea's exports to China stands out. At $16.6 billion, the figure far outpaces the value of shipments to the US. This export pattern reflects two things. On one hand, China's ongoing investment in AI large-language model training, data center construction and digital infrastructure is unleashing enormous demand for memory chips. On the other, Asia's regional semiconductor supply chain retains remarkable resilience despite geopolitical disturbances outside the region. The deep complementarity between the Chinese and South Korean technology industries rests on solid structural foundations. China is one of the world's largest semiconductor markets, with integrated circuit imports rising 63.5 percent year-on-year to $499 billion in the first nine months of this year. Samsung and SK Hynix together hold roughly 70 percent of the global memory chip supplies, and both companies' Chinese plants are deeply embedded in local supply chains. With the world's largest demand market on one side and irreplaceable high-end supply on the other, this deeply intertwined pattern, where each side is present in the other's industrial landscape, is not something that external factors can easily change. But challenges remain behind the eye-catching data. South Korea's chip exports are mostly concentrated in the memory sector. At the same time, the technology export controls implemented by certain countries pose potential risks too. This is precisely why both the space and necessity for deeper China-South Korea industrial chain cooperation are on the rise. If South Korea hopes to translate its current export momentum into sustainable long-term growth, relying solely on technological upgrades and product iteration will not be enough. The more important step lies in proactive industrial chain-level planning, deepening coordination with the broader Asian semiconductor ecosystem, and above all, preserving and expanding the depth of cooperation with China. This is a strategic issue that will determine whether South Korea can retain sufficient room for maneuver in an increasingly fragmented global trade environment. The 17th round of negotiations on Phase II of the China-South Korea Free Trade Agreement, held in Seoul last week, placed services and investment at the core of discussions. This suggests that the two sides may open greater room for institutional opening-up in information technology, high-end manufacturing and the digital economy, extending semiconductor complementarity currently concentrated in goods trade into other fields. Over the medium and long term, complementarity between the Chinese and South Korean industrial chains is far from reaching its ceiling. As global technology supply chains continue to face considerable uncertainty, deeper cooperation grounded in market logic and industrial reality will not only sustain South Korea's export curve, but also inject greater stability into the regional economy.
